utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Licina. Once again I remind you that you are bound by the declaration that you made on the first day to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Licina. Actually if you'll --

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- bear with me, there is one procedural, technical thing that I would like to raise before I get started so I don't forget it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, it deals with Exhibit 881 which was admitted yesterday. The court officer and case manager brought to my attention that a redacted copy needs to be -- needs to replace the unredacted version. It's just a few lines at the top because of the source of this document. It's in e-court. Everything is ready. I just wanted to put it on the record, and if Your Honours approve of that then the court officer will make the necessary change to -- to document -- excuse me, Exhibit 881.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the necessary be done to Exhibit 881, to make sure that we have a redacted version. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: To begin with I'd like to go back, I hope briefly, to the issue of the speech by President Tudjman which we discussed yesterday. Yesterday, I believe -- well, you said that -- you testified that you do remember seeing and hearing that speech and I just wonder if you can describe to me, as best you can, what it was that you think you saw and you think you heard.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a specific sentence. Of course, I didn't attempt to memorise all speeches of Franjo Tudjman but this particular sentence was as follows: There would have been no war had Croatia not wanted one. I am quite familiar with this sentence. It was frequently repeated in various programmes, TV broadcasts. I wasn't referring to a particular speech. I was referring to this particular sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. My question wasn't very well put. I was actually wondering if you could describe where he was or who he was with? Was he standing alone? Was he standing with someone else? Is there any detail like that that you remember about what you think you saw and heard?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: An excerpt from one of his speeches. I don't know it's a speech or an interview. I don't know, but the sentence was very recognisable. It was repeated in many TV broadcasts. So I'm actually speaking about the particular sentence that Franjo Tudjman said that there would have been no war had not Croatia wanted one. There is such a sentence that he stated publicly. It exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You've made very clear what you think the sentence was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, Mr. Milovancevic. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have an objection, Your Honour. I would like for the Chamber to maintain order in the courtroom. Many times I have refrained from making this suggestion. My learned friend Mr. Whiting shakes his head, he's making grimaces with his face, he's laughing. He's sitting between the Prosecutor who is conducting the cross-examination and the witness. So in any case this is something that disturbs me. Mr. Martic also has asked me as his Defence counsel to draw the counsel's attention to this particular thing. We never grimaced. There were a lot of questions which bordered on the ridiculous but we kept our composure, so we would like to ask our colleague, Mr. Whiting, to refrain from such conduct. He is constantly doing this so I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic, for saying so but before I ask Mr. Whiting to say anything I would like to assure you that this Chamber does its very best to maintain order in the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I've reacted, it's been unintentional. I apologise. I don't think it's been constant at all but I'll certainly take care to pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the apology, Mr. Whiting, and I hope you can make sure that it doesn't occur, if it did happen. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, before the interruption, you had made clear what you think you remember as far as the statement and I'm really interested in anything else that you remember, especially visually. Can you give us any context? Was he -- was he standing alone or was he standing with others? Or was he sitting? Any visual clue like that? Can you remember anything about President Tudjman when he was making this statement that you think you saw?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember visually that he was on the screen. I don't know if he was by himself but actually I'm pretty sure that he was by himself. How can I put it? It was a sort of close-up of him. That's what I recall seeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if you can't remember any more, that's fine. I don't mean to push it but can you remember anything about how he was dressed? Was he wearing -- could you tell if he was wearing a coat, was he outside, was he in a shirt, did he have a tie on? Anything like that that you can remember? Just do your best.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that he was wearing just regular clothes that people wear on such occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I'm not asking to you assume or to guess or anything. I want to know what you remember.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as I said, I remember, as far as I can recall, that the statement was broadcast on television, there was a close-up of Franjo Tudjman. I assume that if he's giving a statement like that he's probably wearing just standard clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was probably not wearing his pajamas. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you remember on what occasion this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I said, I don't remember the specific speech. It's one sentence that was later frequently used in different TV broadcasts. There were a number of occasions when this was played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you ever see the whole speech or did you just see a clip of this sentence?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's possible that I did see the entire speech but the -- this particular sentence stuck to my mind. This is what I remember, the sentence was memorable. I don't need to recall all the speeches by Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about any other speech except for this one and I'll just ask you one more time and then we'll move on. I don't want to you guess. I don't want you to assume. Is there anything else, any other detail that you remember about this speech? If there is not, then we'll move on but if there is something else, tell me now.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a memorable sentence. I don't recall any other things right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The Defence last night - I got it this morning but I think it was sent to us last night - has provided us with a newspaper article from the Serbian newspaper, Vesti, which is dated the 16th of June 2006 and I want to show you that article now. So with the assistance of the Court usher, please. I apologise, 16th July. I accidentally said June. But that was an error, the 16th of July 2006. Could I have the assistance of the Court usher to hand him a copy of this, please? I'm sorry, we just got it Your Honour, so this is not in e-court but I have a copy in B/C/S for the witness and then actually I do have an English translation, partial translation which was provided to us by the Defence and so I give copies of that for Your Honour if it's helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. Now, you say this is a newspaper cutting from -- that you received yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct. After our discussion of this speech the Defence e-mailed us this newspaper article with the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, again I have the problem that I'm not familiar with the Cyrillic alphabet so it's not clear to me where on this page the quote is but do you see a quotation of President Tudjman giving a speech on the 24th of May 1992? Do you see that on this page?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's in the last column. It's about halfway down the column, starts with quotations, there would have been no war had Croatia not wanted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: All right. And you can actually -- we can see it because you see the date 24 May 1992, right? That can help us locate it, right about where you were pointing; is that right? Do you see that date there, 24 May 1992 in that same column where you just indicated?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's an interview, I don't see with whom, and the speech is dated on the 24th of May. Whoever is giving the interview dates the speech because I see that there are questions and answers. It's an interpretation, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So this is -- this is an interview with someone and that someone is then recalling this speech and giving their version of the speech; is that what is contained on this page?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He's quoting here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Could you read out that quote which is attributed to President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "There would have been no war had Croatia not wanted it."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And it continues, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "However, we estimated that we can get the independence of Croatia only by war and that is why we conducted a policy of negotiations but behind the negotiations we also prepared for armed conflict." Do you want the whole quote? Shall I read the whole quote?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to read the whole quote again. "There would have been no war had Croatia not wanted it. However, we assess that only we can fight for the independence of Croatia through war. That is why we conducted a policy of negotiations and after that, behind those negotiations we formed armed units. Had we not done that, had we not done that, we would not have reached our objective. It would have been possible to avoid war had we given up on our goals, the independence of our state but this is something that we did not want at the cost of our lives."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, reading this, are those the words that you think you heard Franjo Tudjman say?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably yes, but this is somebody's quote, given in the interview. Yes, I assume that that's what that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Does this affect your opinion on the date? Do you think that maybe the speech that you think you saw or heard was in May 1992 or do you still stand by your testimony yesterday that it was later than that, 1995 or 1996?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I heard that speech in 1995 or 1996. So it's possible. I cannot definitely ascertain the time of that speech. What I was talking about was precisely that sentence. That sentence was used a lot. You could have heard it even over these past few years. It appeared on television. I indicated the time that I heard that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you're saying that it's possible that you saw or you think you saw or heard this clip in 1995 or 1996 but it was really something that was said in May of 1992? That's possible?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, yes. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what you remember seeing or hearing, was it always the same clip or was it different versions? It was always the same clip, I guess, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly it was this excerpt, that there would have been no war had Croatia not wanted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for your help and your patience on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we exhibit this newspaper article, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the newspaper Article please be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number 884.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This doesn't need to have an ERN number and all those things but I'm sure between the Prosecution and the Defence we'll see that that gets done. Since it was provided by them they may want to do it but we are happy to do it. Anyhow we will take care of the technicalities, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Licina. And now I'd like to return just briefly to the issue of United Nations Security Council resolutions, and I'd like to show you one more such resolution. So if we could see on the e-court, please, a document bearing the ERN 00086197 to 6199, please. Again unfortunately I don't a translation of this into B/C/S so it will just be the English that we see but it's a Security Council resolution, number 871, which was adopted the 4th of October 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you waiting for something, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I don't have it on my screen yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, we've had it for quite sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My apologies, then. There, it just came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, do you speak and read any English at all?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can use a little bit of English but I don't really know it that well, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My apologies for not having this in your language. Let me just read out for you a couple of relevant parts. In paragraph 3 of this resolution from October 1993, the Security Council says, "It condemns once again continuing military attacks within the territory of the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and reaffirms its commitment to ensure respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic of Croatia, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia where UNPROFOR is deployed. Then at number 4 it reaffirms the crucial importance of the full and prompt implementation of the United Nations peacekeeping plan for the Republic of Croatia including the provisions of the plan concerning the demilitarisation of the United Nations protected areas and it continues it then it calls on the signatories on the plan to cooperate in its full implementation. In number 6 it calls for an immediate cease-fire agreement between the Croatian government and the local Serb authorities in the UNPAs, and then at 7 it stresses the importance it attaches as a first step towards implementation of the UN peacekeeping plan for the Republic of Croatia to the process of restoration of the authority of the Republic of Croatia in the pink zones. Then it continues a little bit. First, Mr. Licina, this is another example of the Security Council condemning attacks by Croatia in the UNPAs and near the UNPAs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an example when the Security Council again condemns but takes no other steps, even though a number of crimes had taken place. I would like to stress that there were no only crimes committed in the pink zones. At the time of the aggression in the Maslenica area there was an incursion of Croatian forces and 22 soldiers of the RSK were killed in the Mali Alan sector. This was not in a pink zone but it was in the UNPA zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Another part of this document -- well, not another part, one of the parts we read, reaffirms the Security Council's commitment to ensure respect for the sovereignty and the territorial integrity of the Republic of Croatia. And that's because from the international recognition of Croatia, at least at that point in 1992, the Krajina was always viewed by the international community as part of Croatia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Resolution 743, according to which the UNPROFOR forces came to the area of the RSK, was higher by force than these other resolutions. Resolution 743 talked about there being no prejudice for a political solution, that a political solution would be reached by accord, but Croatia violated these agreements and the activities of the UN just boiled down to resolutions such as this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know the date of Resolution 743? Do you remember about the month, for instance?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Resolution 743 is the Vance Plan. I think that it went into force in 1992, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right, but after the international community recognised Croatia, from that point, certainly, although there was -- they said that they weren't going to prejudice any political outcome, they always considered Krajina as part of Croatia, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Resolutions that are of lower rank conflict with Resolution 743 on the basis of which the UNPROFOR forces came to the RSK territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You don't have basis for this claim that one resolution is of a higher or a lower rank than another resolution by the same Security Council, do you? That's just your opinion of those resolutions. You would like that one to have more force than the others.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Resolution 743 was accepted by all the interested parties. Had it not been so, then there would have been no pressure for the Serbs to accept some aspects that were not favourable for them. So in that context, resolution 743 was more important and it did have its political weight or significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right, but in terms of the significance of the resolution, one resolution versus the other, they had the same weight, don't they? What you're talking about is the Vance Plan as an agreement between parties. But the resolutions all have the same weight, don't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They don't have the same weight. Resolution 743 is the implementation of the Vance Plan so they do not have the same weight. I cannot agree with that assertion of yours and I stand by what I have said, that Resolution 743 has a greater degree of weight than the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Another thing that we see in this Security Council resolution, as well as the two that we saw yesterday, is that it calls on the parties, including especially the Serb side, to demilitarise. That was one of the things that the Security Council repeatedly insisted on, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It turns out that you carry out an aggression on an area, you carry out a massacre, and then after that you seek demilitarisation. I think that is cynical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm actually focused on the Serb side because there is - I think you may have talked about - part of the Vance Plan was this idea that the Krajina -- the Serb entity in Krajina had to demilitarise, wasn't supposed to have long-barrelled weapons, for instance. You're familiar with all this, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The demilitarisation process of the Krajina had not even started when the first aggression took place. The deployment of the UNPROFOR forces was not completed when there was aggression in the area of the Miljevac plateau. How can you build confidence and embark on any kind of political negotiations if the other side is absolutely breaking faith?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you there. I think you've answered the question and you keep turning the focus back to the Croatian side but the Serb side never complied with those demilitarisation provisions, did it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had we been demilitarised, then even more of us would have been killed than actually were killed. I don't know what you mean, we should have demilitarised and then we would have been slaughtered in the same way that we were slaughtered in World War II?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether you should or shouldn't have. I'm saying, there was a plan. I'm just wanting you to confirm that the Serb side never complied with that. You never complied with the demilitarisation provisions, did you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those two things are very closely related. You cannot view those things separately. Croatia was the first to begin violating the agreement. It carried the aggression out first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You have made clear that -- about the Croatian aggressions but just answer me: In the context which you've already given, did -- the Serb side never complied with the demilitarisation provisions, did it? Just answer that question. You've given your explanations about the context but answer that question.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until then we were at war and, naturally, confidence is something that has to be earned in order to achieve anything. Croatia provided no grounds to embark on negotiations and to conclude any kind of agreement. So in that position, the Serbs were right not to disarm completely. I assert that had the Serbs disarmed totally, the situation would have been worse. There would have been even more casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You've given the speech but I think in there you said the Serbs were right not to disarm completely. So you're saying the Serbs did not comply with the demilitarisation provisions. Just answer that question, please, and we'll move on to the next one.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Black, you are taking one thing for another. I gave you very clear answers to your questions. The deployment of the UNPROFOR forces hadn't even started when Croatia violated the agreement. That question would make sense had there been a year or two of peace, had there been a certain period of time, and then the Serbs had not disarmed themselves. However, there wasn't really that much time that had passed and the things that happened, happened. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You've given your explanation now four or five times but you won't answer the question. The Serb side did not comply with the demilitarisation provisions, did it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you a very clear answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, you have not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very clear answer, yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: A clear answer would be yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to this type of terror imposed on the witness. The Prosecutor needs to have during cross-examination the response that the witness gave during the examination-in-chief. During examination-in-chief the witness explained that the Serb Territorial Defence presented its heavy weapons under double key to the UN, the tanks, the mortars, but this is another question; we are talking about different things. So let the Prosecutor ask whether he abides by what he said during his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand what you are saying, Mr. Milovancevic. What does the lock and key got to do, and the weapons? The question put to this witness is simple and straightforward. Did the Serb side comply with the demilitarisations? This witness is refusing to answer that question. I don't know what you're talking -- I don't understand your objection and I would like to ask Mr. Black to respond but I must understand what I'm asking him to respond to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness responded to the question by the Prosecutor repeating the same answer several times. The Prosecutor can be satisfied or dissatisfied with that answer but the witness did not back down from what he said during the examination-in-chief. The Prosecutor is questioning the witness about specific situation which happened a year or two years after the implementation of the Vance Plan started and the Prosecution and the Defence both used here resolutions of the UN Security Council where it is stated that the SAO Krajina weapons were placed under double lock and key of the United Nations. But now, the witness has talked about some violations and now based on the answers the Prosecutor is developing some new theories that the Serbs did not disarm. I don't want to comment. This is the right of the Prosecution. But the Prosecutor cannot be allowed to harass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I do have some reply, Your Honour. The first thing I would say is, this is at least the second time where -- when a witness has refused or been unable to answer a question where counsel has taken to his feet and tried to give the answer for the witness. That is not an acceptable form of objection, I would say, but I won't take that any further. As far as I can see, the witness has not answered my question. I put it to him several times. What he does is give a speech or some other kind of explanation but he never answers the question, Your Honour. I certainly will try to tone down -- take it down one step because I don't want to be seen as being overly harsh on the witness but I think the Prosecution is entitled to an answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection is overruled. Answer the question, sir. The question is simply the Serb side did not comply with the demilitarisation orders, did they? Yes or no is the simple answer. We don't need a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian side started the process of demilitarisation and the Croatian side interrupted it with its aggression against the territories of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm afraid that's not an answer to the question put.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand, Your Honour, why it is not an answer. I said that the Serbian side had commenced demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking you did the Serbian side comply with the demilitarisation order? A simple answer to that question is either a yes or a no. No need for a speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you got the answer, Mr. Black? He says yes they did comply with the demilitarisation order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Black, if you will, before you -- I don't know if you're going on to another area but there was a question that arose during the course of your more recent cross-examination that cropped up in my mind that I wanted to get on the record, on the transcript, from the witness. Are you going to go on with this area or were you moving on?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I was just about to move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So could I just please ask this question of the witness? Thank you. Mr. Licina, now, you had spoken in examination-in-chief and you repeated it during cross-examination by Mr. Black, that you considered in part that the UN Security Council was ineffectual and that they merely put out condemnation after condemnation without taking any steps or sanctions against Croatia. Now, in your mind, addressing the situation, what steps ought to have been taken and what sanctions should have been employed against Croatia in the circumstances? What is it that should have been done, based on your position, based on the Serbian position? What should have done that was not done in the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Security Council should have done all in its power to prevent such things from happening. What are the instruments at their disposal? I don't know, I'm not an expert but I know that there is a variety of forms of pressure, from sanctions, of this and that nature. I'm telling you I'm not a specialist but it is a fact that Serbs no longer exist in that territory. That territory has completely been ethnically cleansed from Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could this Resolution 871 which is on our screen please be given an exhibit number and be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The resolution 871 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number 885.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, I'm moving to another subject now. In response to questions from the Defence counsel, you said that you were aware of no parallel structure in the Krajina in 1990, 1991, in the years after that, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you accept that in -- especially in 1990 and 1991, Serbia provided significant amounts of support to the Krajina, to the RSK, in terms of weapons and equipment, personnel, and other kinds of support?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I cannot accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you're not aware of any -- any logistical kind of support that Serbia provided to the SAO Krajina or the RSK?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The support was almost reduced to statements and speeches. People who were natives of the area and people who had family ties came back because it was normal for solidarity to exist on the part of such people. We are fellow countrymen. But nothing of the kind you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you're not aware of any kind of provision of weapons or provision of military support, you're not aware of anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said in my examination-in-chief, only for instance from the depot in Sveti Rok when we lifted the blockade. The mines and explosives from there were withdrawn by the JNA to some other location and we were members of the JNA. That has nothing to do with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you aware -- and were you aware then -- that Serbian Krajina leaders including Mr. Martic had frequent and close contacts with some Serbian leaders from the -- from Yugoslavia, including, of course, Slobodan Milosevic, Jovica Stanisic, Frenki Simatovic. You're aware that there was close and frequent contact between the Krajina leaders and those people, correct? If you're not aware of it, then just say so.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for contacts with Slobodan Milosevic, it was what you could see on television. As for Stanisic and Simatovic, the only link I can make is that both of them had family ties with our area. Stanisic's wife and Stanisic's -- and Simatovic's wife were natives of the area. Simatovic's wife is from Devrnjak [phoen] near Gracac so that was a family tie for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Aside from the family ties you're not aware of any official or political activity by Stanisic or Simatovic in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if you don't know anything more about it, then I'll move on to another subject. At the end of your direct examination, you relied on some figures from an organisation called Veritas. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That organisation is based in Belgrade, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That organisation was set up in 1992 or 1993, I don't remember, in Knin, and it now has headquarters in Belgrade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the head of the organisation is Savo Strbac, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Savo Strbac has publicly defended the innocence of Milan Martic, even go so far as to say that the shelling of Zagreb cannot be considered a crime. Are you aware of those public statements?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember but it's possible that he made a statement like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to hand you a copy of a newspaper article, again this is something which I don't yet have a translation in B/C/S. Actually, I have copies for the Chamber. I'll just read out, Mr. Licina, the quotation here. It's towards the bottom of this article. This is an article, by the way, dated the 16th of May, from the SRNA news agency in Bijeljina, and it says, "If Martic issued an order to shell Zagreb, that means he did so out of extreme need, in order to eliminate the simultaneous and obvious danger to the people of Western Slavonia which cannot be considered a criminal act." And that's Savo Strbac talking. Did you ever hear any statements like that from Mr. Strbac?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember but he could have said that. I don't remember this specific statement but I'm not saying he was incapable of saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, I'll put to you, then, that relying on figures from Mr. Strbac, that's not a very objective source, is it? Someone who has come out publicly in defence of the accused, Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, the figures of Savo Strbac on casualties and victims are certainly smaller than Serbian casualties because he comes from Gracac municipality and I know that in that municipality, 500 people got killed in that municipality. I think Strbac has a lower figure. In Veritas's documentation --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you explained those figures earlier on; I won't ask you to repeat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this be admitted into evidence, please, this article?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number 886.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, I'm nearly finished with my questions. You're a member of the RSK government in exile still today, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We started working again on the 26th of February last year, and I'm one of the ministers of this cabinet in exile.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Slobodan Jarcevic is another member of that government in exile; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Jarcevic is an adviser to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And Milan Martic is still the president of that government in exile, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Martic is the president of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And your government in exile is the government of the RSK, right? That's your position, anyhow?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The first minister is Mr. Milorad Buha.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the goal of your government in exile, I take it, is to re-establish the RSK in Croatia, where it was declared in 1991, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective of our government is to redefine Croatia. The objective of our government is for the refugee Serbs from Croatia to come back, over 600.000 of them. Another objective of the exile government is to reclaim 50.000 Serbian flats, to rebuild Serbian houses, to reclaim various rights of the Serbs and get compensation for Serbs of over 60 billion euros in indemnities, and to restore for the Serbs the status of a constituent people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And also, to re-establish the RSK, right? That's why you're a government in exile, not just some non-governmental organisation. You're saying you're the government. You want to re-establish that political entity, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We set to ourselves the maximum ambitious objectives and what time will bring and what we will be able to do, we will see. In politics, everybody sets maximum goals and achieves as much as they manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And among those maximum ambitious objectives that you've set for yourself is the re-establishment of the RSK, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one of the objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you on the e-court system a document with the ERN 06030297 to 0301. This is actually a document that contains both an English and B/C/S version in the original. It's not a translation that we've done. If we can just look at that first page, perhaps. The witness as well, because I don't know that the address appears in the B/C/S version. But Mr. Licina, this is a letter -- actually, if we could turn to the last page real quickly. I'd like to see who signed this.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it in English here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Hopefully it just turned to the last page which is in B/C/S. It's actually -- it's a letter in two languages so it starts in English and the last few pages are in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, since Mr. Licina just said the text was in English, the Defence has a copy of this in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it now in B/C/S on the screen. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Maybe it would be easiest if I get him a hard copy. I'll see if I have one. It will only take me two seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He's got the B/C/S on the screen. That's correct, Mr. Licina; is that correct? You've got the B/C/S on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could just flip again to the last page of the B/C/S, I just want to see who this letter is from. It just appears -- that's you, right, Mr. Licina? Ratko Licina, that's who is the author of this letter?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And this is a letter -- perhaps now if we'll turn to the first page of the document, this is a letter that was actually sent to the United States of America House of Representatives; is that right? Actually --

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just raise it a bit, to Frederick Peterson, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's correct. And on the first page which is in English but it shows -- I can just read it to you. It says, "Mr. Frederick Peterson III, JD, Senior Policy Adviser, US State House Representative, Washington DC." Do you remember this letter that you sent to him in October of 2005?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I just want you to look at a couple of passages. The first one is in that first paragraph which you see on your screen now. I'll just read out a sentence. Following along with me. It says, "We hope that you will contribute so that the revealed truth helps to remove the world's informative blockade about the suffering of the Serbian people -- suffering which is incomparably bigger than the suffering of Albanians in Kosovo, Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatians in Croatia." And then a little bit further down in the second paragraph after it says, "Dear Mr. Peterson" again, it says, "The biggest ethnical cleansing on the Balkans was performed on Serbian people -- 80 per cent of Serbs from Croatia and the majority from Kosovo and Metohija was exiled." And then if we skip down a couple of paragraphs, you'll have to turn to the next -- actually, there is one that starts with, "the suffering of Serbs in Croatia is even bigger." Do you see that there, Mr. Licina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just zoom in a bit? It's page 4. Does it say 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we mean the same sentence, it's the end of page 3 in B/C/S, judging by the words quoted by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually I'll just read out --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still see page 4. And I need 3, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It starts at the beginning, the bottom of this page and it will continue on to the top of the next page. Just led me read out. It says, "Suffering of Serbs in Croatia is even bigger. Nor in this country is respected private property. Croatia has retrieved citizenship from Serbs and the status of constitutional population. Croatia was two nationalities, a state: vote in parliament took away the right of citizenship from Serbs." And it goes down, at the end of this paragraph where it says, "The same injustice to Serbs is repeated now in The Hague Tribunal because in the accusations against Serbs, it is written that Serbs have 'participated in aggression to Croatia or Bosnia and Herzegovina.' Injustice will be even bigger if the Tribunal cedes some cases against to Croatian or Bosnian courts as it has been announced. Serbs have been the owners of a land in the Republic of Serbian Krajina (UN protection zones) too but the world's medias presented those Serbs also as aggressors." Is that -- is that a pretty close translation, at least?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that statehood was taken away from Serbs that their status of a state-forming constituent nation, and it says Serbs could not have been aggressors in Bosnia and Herzegovina as they were portrayed. I think those are the two inaccuracies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. You still hold all these views today, right? You stand by what is written in this letter about the suffering of the Serb people and the biggest ethnic cleansing in the Balkans against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, I stand by it. I don't see that any of that has changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your positions on this really haven't changed at all since 1990, 1991, 1992, since that time. You still hold basically the same views now as did then, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that is consistent on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number 887.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Licina. I have no further questions for you. Your Honour, I believe it's time for the break, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. That's a very timely ending. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, the Defence has a few questions for you relating to some of the questions put to you by the Prosecutor. One of the last questions put to you referred to the government in exile. You explained that you are a member of that government. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphones for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you remind us when you left the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left Krajina in August 1995. I think it was the 5th or the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And the reason you left the Krajina was?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason why I left Krajina was the aggression by Croatia on the Krajina region, the region of northern Lika, Kordun, Lika and Banija specifically, and that operation is known as Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened to the members of the assembly of the RSK? You mentioned them in relation to the government in exile. Did they stay in Krajina or did they also leave?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was one of the deputies of that assembly myself that was elected in late 1993. And, yes, all the deputies of the RSK assembly left the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your responses during the examination-in-chief and also in relation to this topic of the government in exile, you explained that you lived in Gracac. Can you tell us where you lived in Gracac and did you own any property?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in Zagreb up until 1990, then I returned to Gracac. I returned, we had a flat, my mother had a flat in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you still own that apartment?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the apartments owned by the Serbs have not been returned. Actually, 50.000 Serbs had tenant rights to the same number of apartments and this right has now been denied to them. The Croats managed to secure their ownership rites to these apartments but not the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have one more question. You are now in Belgrade. Do you have an apartment in Belgrade now? What is your status there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm living in Belgrade. Specifically I live in Zemun and I don't own my own apartment. I am renting an apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: 11 years after Storm, are you a citizen of Croatia, Serbia or of any other country? What is your status? Could you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the status of a refugee in Serbia. I am not a citizen of any state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have now finished with this topic of the government in exile, Mr. Licina. I'm going to put some other questions to you regarding Mr. Raskovic. You recall that my learned friend from the Prosecution, in the cross-examination, showed you excerpts from the book, "Crazy Land" of professor academician, Raskovic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that the Prosecutor also showed you an excerpt of the text citing Mr. Raskovic about how the Ustasha movement is a rational delirium, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also showed you a text in which Mr. Raskovic, continuing with this remark, says that the Ustashas as early as 1940, planned the destruction of the Serbs and they listed all the pits in Croatia. Do you recall that sentence?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to that, can you tell us what these pits are in Croatia? Are they holes, pits, hollows dug by people or what are they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pits are places in Croatia where executions were carried out and Serb bodies were thrown in during World War II. There are many such pits. One is close to where I live. It's called Turcic. One of the most famous of these or notorious of these pits is a pit called Jadovno but there are many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So did Mr. Raskovic speak the truth about this when he wrote that these pits were also dealt with in the planning process of genocide? Do you agree that these pits existed where bodies of people were thrown in?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with what Mr. Raskovic said. I think most people know about this and they would agree with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit 65 ter 298 on the monitor? It's a map. It's probably been given an exhibit number but I don't have that number available right now so perhaps we could have that on the monitors, please. Could we please zoom in on the lower right quadrant of the map? Could we look at the entire green area, please?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit yellow, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right. This is a document used before this Trial Chamber. Could you please read what it says in the upper right-hand corner, Mr. Licina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "Map of the Ustasha genocide of the Serbian people in the territory of the Independent State of Croatia from 1941 to 1945."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we scroll the map up a little bit so that we can see the key? Actually, could we scroll down - I'm not sure if I'm giving the right instructions - so that we see the bottom of the map? On the left side, it said, "key." Could you please read us the elements of the key?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The locations of the Ustasha genocide were marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, when you read the text, the text is next to a marking. So can you please tell us what marking you see and the text?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first little circle says that these are locations of Ustasha genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then there is a sort of larger encircled space. It says, "Areas where there was mass genocide carried out of the Serbian people." Then I can't really see it so well but these look like blue arrows or something like that. "Concentration and collection camps." Then there is a larger black spot, "Pits where Serbs were thrown." Then there is a red triangle next to which it says, "Wells where Serbs were thrown in."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Licina. Can we look at the map again on the monitor, the map that is just above the text and the legend, the key? Thank you. Do you see these small dots on the map? Do you see these bigger black dots on the map? Do you see the red try angles? Actually the markings whose definitions you read in the key?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What does this map in front of you represent? Do you recognise this territory?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I can see, this is the territory of the Independent State of Croatia from World War II. It encompasses the territory of the former socialist Republic of Croatia and the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the right-hand side, there is some writing and it's quite small. I don't want to make you read that from the screen. It's quite small. I'm going to read it, so if you can perhaps follow. The text says, "The German authorised general in the Independent State of Croatia, Edmund Gleise Von Horstenau, who is a historian, writes that 'the Ustashas claimed that 1 million Orthodox Serbs were slaughtered, children, women, and the elderly,' and that, according to him, 'this is exaggerated, because, on the basis of reports received, the number of those slaughtered was actually three-quarters of a million.'" Is this what it says in this text, Mr. Licina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under that, it is said that the author who drafted this text, Mr. Miletic, did that in his book, The Ustasha Death Factory: 1941 to 1945.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have one question in relation to this text that I read to you, Mr. Licina. Can you please tell us what three-quarters of a million is, what number is that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you calculate three-quarter of a million is 750.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The envoy of Hitler's Germany in the Independent State of Croatia says that in the territory of that state from 1941 to 1945, 750.000 people were slaughtered. Is he using the correct term when he says slaughtered? What do you mean about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, he's using the correct term. He's using the term, "had their throats cut." According to what I know, the Ustashas in the camps and next to the pits cut the throats of people. That's how they executed people. There were also cases when there were sort of competitions between Ustashas who would cut the throats of more people in a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need to use this map any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you carry on, Mr. Milovancevic, can you just remind me, do we have this map in English? The English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is Exhibit number 492. I'm sorry I did not give you the reference to the English text because the -- because we were using the actual map but if necessary, I can provide that for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've just been told there is an English copy of that map. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, you saw many dots on this map. These are locations where, according to this map and according to what you said, Serb bodies were thrown in. Mr. Raskovic talked about that in his book, "Luda Zemlja," "Mad Country." In the paragraph shown to you by the Prosecutor. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor was particularly interested in the use of the term or the sentence, "The Ustasha movement is also a rational delirium." Do you recall that sentence?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You answered that Mr. Raskovic was a neuropsychiatrist by profession, that he was probably doing that from a professional aspect. So could we now please look at Exhibit 874 on our monitors? And that is the text, "Mad country," by Mr. Jovan Raskovic. Could we please look at page 1? And it bears the indication 92927454. This is the B/C/S version. In English, it's also on the -- page 1. It's the next page after the title page. Could we please look at that on our monitors? The Prosecutor pointed you to the paragraph before last on the left side and it's on this side of the B/C/S text, and it says, "The Ustasha movement is also a rational delirium." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This part of the text was translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to Your Honours and to my learned friends from the Prosecution because I do not have the translation of the paragraph above the one that was shown to you. In that part, Mr. Raskovic explains what rational delirium is and how it is formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So could we please have you read that text? It's a little bit longer. Could you please read it slowly so that the interpreters could translate that and then we will present that as an exhibit and after that we are going to look at the English translation. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "From ideology. Ideology forms and creates a rational delirium. It is a form of fantasy which is directed, that is how there was rational delirium in Nazi-ist ideology. In order to implement it needed to be rationalised. Irrational delirium would be very ineffective. If the task was to destroy Jews and Slavs, then that delirious idea had to be given a rational form in order to be able to implement all of that. First, victims needed to be prevented in one way and they needed to be stripped of their human characteristics and thus create conditions for their destructions. In the slaughterhouse and the concentration camp, this delirious basis was rationalised, chauvinism and racism used to a large extent rational delirium because rational delirium is very - quote, unquote - useful to the masses. What is happening now in Kosovo and Metohija (rapes, all the aggression towards neighbours, all those inappropriate things, all the shame) are all actually rational delirium."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if it's technically possible for this part of the text that you read, since we only have the B/C/S text, if you can circle that with a pencil. If possible, could the usher please help you to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I have read? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. Licina.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I know that the interpreters interpreted what the witness was reading but do we have a translated portion, a translated version of that portion that you read, because I couldn't see it on the English version when I was listening to the witness and the English version is only two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is exactly what I tried to explain. My learned friend, the Prosecutor, showed the witness some other sections of the text and they were translated. This section of the text that is circled now is just above the text used by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that portion. I understand that part. I understand you. My question to you is, do you have a translated version of the portion that you now used today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have it at this moment. I wanted just to have this part of the text marked and we will provide the translation in due course. That is, as soon as we can. That's all I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you to do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just one question before I tender this part of this statement to be exhibited as a Defence Exhibit. When you said that Mr. Raskovic spoke about the rational delirium as an expert, as a psychiatrist, when you were responding to the Prosecutor's question whether you thought that it could be an explanation, is this what explains your answer?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We see a lot of specialised terminology here. This text practically is targeted at experts more than a broader public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this be exhibited as a Defence Exhibit and can we give it a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That portion of the document is admitted into evidence as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 888.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We don't need this text on the monitor any more. Thank you, Mr. Usher; I believe we have dealt with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm advised that that image has not been saved because of a technical problem. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, regarding the questions asked of you by -- concerning Mr. Raskovic, this text and some other speeches, my question is: You were a member of the executive board of the party, even the main board of the party, I suppose you met with Mr. Raskovic, and I want to know on the basis of what you know of him, of his public and political life? Could you draw the conclusion that he was a nationalist, a Serb nationalist?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in which sense you mean this term, Serb nationalist. In a positive sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I was not precise enough. When I said nationalist, I meant the possibly extremist attitude that is expressed as hatred towards other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean as a chauvinist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a chauvinist?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then no, Jovan Raskovic could by no means be called a chauvinist. As far as I know, his wife was a Croat and he often emphasised that point in his speeches. And what we actually called Mr. Raskovic was Serbian Gandhi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move to another subject, namely the commitments of the HDZ expressed in its platform and its statute. Do you remember the Prosecutor's questions about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we see on our screens Exhibit 873? That is a document of the Croatian Democratic Union from 1990. This document was seen by all of us, including you, yesterday. The Prosecutor put this document to you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, twice, as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see page 8 in B/C/S? In English it's page 7. In the left side of the text, in B/C/S, we see on the monitor, can we zoom in on the left hand bottom corner? There we see the Roman numeral 2 and the subheading reads, "About the unequivocalness of the programmes. Objectives of the Croatian Democratic Union." The last paragraph in this paragraph is, and reads, I'll read it. It's difficult to follow because it moves on to the other page, "This proceeds from the very fact that this programme and policies are being built by us, apart from the general democratic principles of modern civilisation, on the three major components of the recent Croatian history, on the Starcevic Croatian historic state," right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's request we have not finished interpreting the excerpt. Can we please stop with the question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, the interpreter just asked you to hold on a little bit there. They have not finished interpreting the text of that document you are reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for the interruption. If we are going to read at length from this, I do have two extra copies that perhaps could be given to the interpreters. It might help their tasks. I don't know if that's helpful or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It may very well be helpful because the interpreters is not exactly the same as here as I understand it means the same thing but the words are not the same and it makes it a little difficult even for us to follow where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I avail myself of this opportunity to ask the interpreters to always caution me when necessary. At some points, I lose track of the fact that I may be too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They always do. May we ask you, in return, Mr. Milovancevic, to try to always remember not to be too fast? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This piece we read or interpreted before is on page 7 of the English version and it is paragraph 3, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Does the Trial Chamber want to have it read now? Or is the text enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe if -- no. The text will be enough. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, Mr. Licina, since you did mention Ante Starcevic as a Croatian politician, what was his attitude towards Serbs? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Starcevic was a Croatian politician of the 19th century, if I remember correctly. He led the Croatian Party of Rights and otherwise he was known for his very rigid attitude towards Serbs. There was one quotation from his works saying that they are dogs that need to be axed down. He simply thought there existed no Serbs in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We saw that Mr. Tudjman based the programmed objectives of the HDZ on his views, Starcevic's views, but we will go on reviewing the programmed goals of the HDZ. In the last paragraph on the monitor now in front of you, the end of the right-hand side, which is page 9 in B/C/S, in English it's pages 7 and -- in fact the last paragraph on page 7, and it goes on, on page 8. I hope I have identified this portion of the text precisely. Mr. Licina, could you please read for us in this paragraph from the second sentence? We need to show on the monitor page 10 in B/C/S. The sentence begins, "At the same time they are forgetting."

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At the same time, they are forgetting that the NDH, the Independent State of Croatia, was not just a quisling creation and a fascist crime but also an expression of both the Croatian historic aspirations for an independent state but also the realisation of these aspirations on the part of international factors, in this particular case Hitler's Germany, that created a new European order on the ruins of the Versailles order. Therefore, the NDH was not merely a mere whim of the powers of the Axis but also a result of quite defined historic factors."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your answers during examination-in-chief, when you mentioned the speech of Mr. Tudjman at the Vatroslav Lisinski hall, did you mean this text?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely. This speech was held in the Vatroslav Lisinski hall, namely the founding assembly of the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this text, Mr. Tudjman, and that is the gist of this sentence, it says, "At the same time, they are forgetting that the NDH was not just a quisling creation and a fascist crime but also an expression of the historic aspirations of Croatia." Now, is this the same Croatia that we saw marked with those pits in the form of triangles and black dots?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the only state during the Second World War, apart from Hitler's Germany, which had concentration camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Picking up on the questions of the Prosecutor as to whether the HDZ was a democratic party or whether it expressed its xenophobia and also questions about its aspirations, let us look at page 39 of this document. In English it would be page 34. When we see it on the screen, you will see that it is an electoral proclamation of the HDZ to the citizens of Croatia and the entire Croatian people. So it's page 39 on B/C/S. In this part of the text, we also find the portion put to you by the Prosecutor, the portion that speaks about what one gains by giving one's vote to the HDZ. There are 27 or 28 points here, and it's somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this, voting for the HDZ, you are voting for?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please, look at -- read for us, in fact, points 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Voting for the HDZ, you are voting for, 1, the incontestable, non-transferrable, interminable and indivisible sovereignty of the Croatian people, in keeping with the general achievements of modern humanity and with the Charter of United Nations. 2, for the current and inalienable right of the entire Croatian nation within their historical and natural borders to self-determination after secession and to" -- can we see the entire page and zoom it in? "To self-determination up to -- up to secession and to contractual arrangements of relations with neighbouring nations in the present SFRY and Europe."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: From these provisions of this proclamation that you've just read, does your knowledge, while you were in Zagreb, that in Gracac and its territory of SAO Krajina, does your knowledge confirm that one of the programmed objectives of the HDZ was to ensure sovereignty for the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I refrained from the last two questions or two questions before this that I think were leading but this -- I think this is a leading question, Your Honour. He could get the answer in a non-leading way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not want to ask leading questions. Maybe they appear so and if they appear so, then I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is a leading question, Mr. Milovancevic. Yes, you must withdraw that question and rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will withdraw the question and rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The question is: In its electoral proclamations, did the HDZ advocate gaining sovereignty for the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we see from this proclamation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at item 14 of this proclamation? What else are you voting for by voting for the HDZ, according to this electoral proclamation? It's a very brief sentence.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 14, "for integration of Croatia with Europe, a Croatia as a sovereign and modern state."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was one of the main goals of the HDZ and their policy at the time, including the pre-electoral rallies?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear from this proclamation of theirs, as well as from their pre-election rallies, that their platform primarily was to rearrange the then federal state or rather to secede from Yugoslavia, and they also wanted to do away with the rights of Serbs, the right to their statehood within the boundaries of Croatia and subsequently within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We can now remove this document. During the cross-examination, the Prosecutor asked several questions concerning the declaration adopted in Srb dated the 25th of July 1990, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please have that declaration on the monitor? This is Exhibit 141. While we are waiting for the document, I wanted to ask you this: And perhaps you can provide us with a brief answer.
