According to your knowledge, the Yugoslav constitution, back in 1990, did it foresee the right of individual peoples to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to the Yugoslav constitution which peoples, which nations, have that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs, Croats, Slovenians, Macedonians, Montenegrins, and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct if I state that now you've numbered the Yugoslav nations which had the right to self-determination?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not individual citizens but the various nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the text of the declaration before you and read the third paragraph within item 1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which declaration are we now reading, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the declaration from Srb adopted at the Serb meeting there on the 25th of July 1990, which is Exhibit -- and this is in front of you -- that is Exhibit 141. It has been admitted, and the Prosecutor asked several questions of the witness concerning the declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This declaration on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serb people, what does it state in its third paragraph of item 1?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have page 1 of this declaration, and it is item 1, its third paragraph. The text begins with, "One cannot"?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "One cannot choose the type of Yugoslav federation without the participation of the Serb people in Croatia and this particularly goes for situations of legitimate secession. Nations secede, not states."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday by the Prosecutor whether you believe that the Serbs in Croatia had the right to veto Croatia's secession. To go back to that topic, I wanted to ask you this: Do you believe that the Croatian people in the then Socialist Republic of Croatia had the right to secede and did they have the right to their own state?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never tried to deny the right of the Croatian people to self-determination. That was never in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that the Serb people have the same right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the same token, yes. The Serbs had the right to self determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute ago, we saw the electoral proclamation of the HDZ, inviting the citizens of Croatia to give their votes to the HDZ to establish the independent Croatian state which would secede from Yugoslavia. Is this how you interpreted the text of the proclamation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we take a look at the proclamation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, once again you are leading. You are telling him the answer and having told him the answer you say, "Is this how you interpret it?" And while we are at it, Mr. Milovancevic, and I don't want to interfere with your re-examination, I hope if you could try to stick to clarifying issues that were not clear rather than re-examining him as if you are leading him in chief again. But please don't lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You just told us what you thought was the goal of the HDZ policy as regards Croatia, stemming from their proclamation. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that the rights of those who wish to leave a certain country carry more weight than the rights of those who wish to stay, to remain within? What is your view?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rights have to be balanced of both those who wish to leave and those who wish to stay, and as was actually foreseen by the federal constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The third paragraph of item 1 of the declaration you've just read out, does that set out or define an attitude different from the one you just stated?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it tallies with what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes this particular topic, Mr. Licina. During your -- yesterday's testimony you were shown a part of your speech given at the assembly of the Republika Srpska Krajina which was held in Beli Manastir; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the monitor you circled a sentence in which you mentioned Ustashas three times?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember being asked by the Prosecutor about your use of terms from World War II in 1990 and 1991, precisely by mentioning the word Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we now please see a video footage prepared by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could that be repeated because at first it only came partially on the screen so I was not really able to see all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: "... [indiscernible] co-leader of the Croatian death squads was Branimir Glavas. Unlike more discreet members of the ruling HDZ party, Glavas made no secret of his identification with the World War II Croatian Ustashas as he welcomed returning Croatian prisoners of war. While some French --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It is a short footage. And I would like to lend a hand to the Chamber and to the witness so as to be able to understand what the aim of my question is. Could we have the usher distribute the copies of this text uttered by a person in the footage? Perhaps you could give that to the Chamber and to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters be given a copy as well? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is just a very brief passage. It is one sentence only, and perhaps the interpreters will do without the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, do you see the date on the screen, the date of the footage?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, it is the 9th of August 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In front of you, on the screen, there is a flag. Can you tell us what or whose flag that is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the Croatian flag with the -- their coat of arms, identical to the one used during World War II. It is the same as the Ustasha flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say this is the Croatian flag with the coat of arms, why do you specify that? Why did you describe it in that way?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we see the coat of arms in the centre of the white portion. It's a chequerboard and the difference between the Ustasha coat of arms and the one used nowadays is that the Ustasha coat of arms began in the upper left corner with the white square.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did this particular flag begin appearing in the territory of Croatia and what did the previous flag look like?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The previous flag was the same in terms of colours, but the official socialist Republic of Croatia flag had the five-pointed star in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this footage, you saw a person uttering a sentence. Do you remember what he said? Could we play this again so as to be able to see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: "... identification with the World War II Croatian Ustasha as he welcomed returning Croatian prisoners of war. While some French --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Black is on list feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. I notice that there is no date at the time when he's making the speech. The date seems to come from the shot of the flag but it seems that we have several different events put together. So if we could have a date and maybe a source for that, the clip where the person is actually speaking, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these were precisely the questions I wanted to ask of the witness, and I will try to have that clarified by the witness himself, in particular the question to the Prosecutor's -- the answer to the Prosecutor's question, and then the Defence may provide further clarifications if necessary. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did this gentleman say? Do you remember it? Can you paraphrase it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. There is Branimir Glavas. Branimir Glavas used to be a highly positioned person within the HDZ, and at the same time he was in the parliament when I was in the Croatian parliament as well. He was one of the deputies. This footage in which he said, "Feel free to say that you are Ustashas because you indeed are and welcome to your state," I am pretty sure that this was at an exchange of prisoners. I believe this was in 1991, around Vukovar or Osijek, because at that time he was in that area. As far as I know, he also has a high position in Osijek nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right to say that we can see this Branimir Glavas in the footage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, ask him to show you Mr. Glavas. Don't say, "Am I right," because you're going to lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I withdraw my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The person addressing these people spoke to them as they were moving in a column. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said previously, this was an exchange of prisoners during the conflict. These were Croatian prisoners exchanged for Serbian prisoners and they were crossing over to the Croatian territory. Branimir Glavas welcomed them with the following words, "Feel free to say that you are Ustashas because indeed you are and you are now back home. You are in your own state."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see this footage for the first time or were you able to see it sometime earlier?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where was it broadcast?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On many TV programmes. On both Croatian and the RTS television, one could see this footage often, and this precedes my speech we discussed that occurred in 1993. This is a high Croatian official who confirmed that, indeed, they were Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what is happening in Croatia with Mr. Glavas today?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there is a trial underway in Zagreb relating to the killings of Serbs in the Osijek region, because he was in charge in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to have this video footage tendered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The video footage is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number 889.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We do not need to see the footage any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: During yesterday's cross-examination, my learned friend from the Prosecution showed you a document that is one page of the Vreme magazine and the date in the lower left-hand corner was the 27th of January 1992. On that page, you see the text that Jovan Raskovic talked about. There is one sentence, "I feel responsible because I carried out preparations for the war even though I did not do that voluntarily." Do you recall that one sentence?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at this page of text on the monitor, please? This is Exhibit 879. Do you recognise this text?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the right-hand column, there is a second photograph. It shows a man with a beard. Do you recognise that man?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is academician Jovan Raskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On this page, please look at the first column to the left. We don't see all of it. Can we see the beginning of the left column and also this photograph? That is right. Could you please zoom in a little bit of the -- on the photograph that is in the left-hand column? The text is in B/C/S. We do not have a translation. Mr. Licina, could you please tell us what it says above this photograph? And what it says beneath the photograph?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Below the photograph it says, "Marko Perkovic Thompson, Croatian guard and composer."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of such a person?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard about Thompson. I've heard of him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who is he and what is he wearing? Could you please describe that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's wearing a uniform. His nickname, Thompson, is something that he got because of the weapon that you can see him carrying in his arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since we don't all have to know what a Thompson is, could you please tell us what is a Thompson?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thompson is an automatic weapon. It's an automatic rifle. It's a little bit old in manufacture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at the photograph -- the text underneath the photograph, please? Thank you. We can stop here. Could you please read the title in quotes, in the bold letters?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Fighter from Cavoglava."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what does this title indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a term that was used for Ustasha soldiers, Bojovniks in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Underneath that text, there is the first line of text. Could you please read that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first line reads, "za dom -- spremni," "ready for the homeland."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us if you've heard of that expression and what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The expression, "za dom -- spremni," is a term used by Croatian Ustashas. It was a greeting, just like German Nazis greeted one another with "Heil Hitler," the Croatian Ustashas greeted one another by using the term, "za dom -- spremni."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Underneath that text, "za dom -- spremni," about the middle of the text, there is a piece of text that says, "Thompson is hitting and also the Kalashnikov." Is this a poem?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a poem because he's a poet of sorts and it says, [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is a little bit hard to translate this poem by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us what this band of Chetniks is and what is this justice that's going to get to them, to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cavoglava is an area that is very close to the RSK, and in this text, the locations of Baljci and Mirlovici are being mentioned. These are actually Serbian last names that bordered on this territory, so he's sending a message from the border areas to Serbs and he's talking about their closest neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the part of the poem above that so that it's a little bit closer, so that we understand a little bit more what it says?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The witness quotes the poem in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And then it says we will reach you, even in Serbia. Could you please read the very end of this text? Can we look at the end of this text that is in the text box. The text is in parentheses.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The poem Bojovnik from Cavoglava last week was declared as the most popular patriotic number in Croatia last week on the Croatian radio programme, the Split Studio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to have this document, this column, marked with a separate number and could we please tender that as an exhibit? We will get a translation of this poem and I would like to seek the Chamber's understanding. I didn't have too much time and there were a lot of documents I had to cover stemming from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, this whole document is in. If they want to certainly no problem to translate -- for them to get a translation of the poem part as well as we will get the translation of the other part but I don't think it needs to be a separate exhibit unless the Chamber feels otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you happy with that arrangement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is logical, Your Honours. Yes, I agree. I actually forgot that this document has already been tendered. It's fine, thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe what could be done is to circle that poem and save it now this time with the poem circled just to remind ourselves that that's one of the things that needs to be translated. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we are circling this part of the text and in order to avoid misunderstanding, maybe it would be good then to have that as a separate exhibit, the circled text, because below that there is also the date as well as the indication which magazine this was published in and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And may I take the opportunity to ask about the nature of this magazine? What kind of magazine is it and where was it published? Can you explain that? Can you explain that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll this up a little bit? If I'm not mistaken -- can we scroll up? I think this is the magazine Vreme. This is a Belgrade weekly. Can I just look at the date, please? Can you scroll up, please? Yes, the 27th of January 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If it's of assistance, Your Honour, maybe the easiest way is the Prosecution -- we will ask for a translation of all the text on this page and that way this could just stay in as one exhibit as it is now and we'll have a translation of all the words on the entire page. If that's easiest. I just offer it as a possible solution but I'm happy with whatever Your Honour prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excepting that the middle column has not been dealt with in this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will have translated -- we could have the whole page translated for completeness or we can have the column that the Prosecution referred to as well as this entire box that contains the poem. We can do that and it will just be excerpts from that page. If you prefer, the Prosecution will request that translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay. So be it. So we can get the document off the screen now without giving it any exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I say I don't think we don't have a translation of the right piece also.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. It's been requested but we'll modify the request so that it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I do need a clarification as well of the transcript. At page 55, line 5 it says "the poem last week was declared as the most popular patriotic number in Croatia last week on the Croatian radio programme, the Split Studio." Is that the poem or the poet? "The poem last week was declared as the most popular patriot."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was the poem, the word "number" refers to the poem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does that mean that the poem is a patriot?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Patriotic poem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may indeed proceed, Mr. Milovancevic. I beg your pardon. Would that be a convenient moment? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm planning to move to a different topic any way, Your Honour, so this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will then take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, we are going to move to another topic that was covered by the Prosecutor. Do you recall that my learned friend from the Prosecution asked you about your stay in Zagreb at the Assembly of the Republic of Croatia in your capacity as a deputy in late August 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that he showed you newspaper report referring to your participation in the work of that assembly session and that he showed you the text that you actually -- that was your address, that related to the Serbian and Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at Exhibit 880 on our monitors, please? Until we see the text, can you please just listen? I'm going to remind you that this text was published in the Croatian newspaper, Vjesnik, on Saturday the 25th of August 1990. Can you tell us, Vjesnik, where is that published?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vjesnik is a Zagreb daily. It's published in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have not turned my monitor on and I'm waiting for the text to come on now. I understand that. You can see this text in front of you now, the heading -- can you please read the heading above the -- this is the subheading.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Extraordinary session of the Croatian assembly."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The third vertical column from the left to the right contains the text showed to you by the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but could we please zoom in on that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It's the middle part of that column. Excellent, excellent.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subheading is opposition as an operetta set.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now you are talking about the political entities, the Croatian and Serbian people as political peoples. Could you please read the last sentence of this section in the middle column? You read the part that related to the Croatian and Serbian political people, that they formed a little bit later according to Starcevic's political projects. Could you please read the continuation of that sentence?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Serbian political people should have the same right as the Croatian people in this republic," and then in these -- in the parentheses it says, "assembly deputies began the Serbian political people should have the same right as the Croatian people in this state," and then in parentheses it says, "the assembly members began to boo and whistle following these remarks."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me if that is what you said on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This quote has been correctly conveyed. It's exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And was it correctly reported that you, as a member of the Croatian assembly, a Croatian deputy, you were booed by the Croatian assembly members?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Also, the same experience, my colleague Radoslav Tanga had the same experience in September when a briefcase was actually thrown at him in the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now to read the next paragraph. It begins with the subtitle, "Night refugee columns recall war." Could you please read this text to the end, that is on this page?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please scroll the text up?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And could we also zoom in on the end of the third column? Can you scroll in the opposite direction? Scroll down, please. Could you read that part of the text?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my name onwards?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Ratko Licina went on to say that the Serbian political people would have all the rights if this republic were historical and democratic. However, it's neither historical nor democratic. If anybody attacked democracy in these territories of ours, then that would be the state with all of its police states. The democratic right of the national Serbian plebiscite was -- in response to that there was the force of the state apparatus directed at it."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We will no longer be needing to read any more from the text. Did you actually say what you are allegedly quoted as having said here, Mr. Licina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you were speaking at the assembly, as a deputy of that assembly, is that -- were you speaking the truth then?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That was on the 25th of July 1990. Were there any reactions to your speech by the Croatian parliament or maybe other authorities in terms of finding a solution to the problem?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian authorities did not attempt to solve any problems. Problems, on the contrary, continued to grow and as for reactions in the Croatian parliament itself, they were described here and this went on throughout my speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, does this sentence mean anything to you, I am happy with that my wife is neither a Serb nor a Jew?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the sentence. It was uttered by Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when he uttered it and what capacity he had at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was already elected at that time as president of the Republic of Croatia, the then socialist Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend from the Prosecution asked you several times whether the Serb people in Croatia had their fears stoked by the new Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their fears were stoked by the Croatian authorities with their statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Hold it. Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, I don't know if it's an objection. I think it may be an interpretation error. I'm not sure -- what we heard, what was translated into English, is that the Serb people in Croatia had their fears stoked by the new Croatian authorities. Perhaps counsel said Serbian authorities. If he said Croatian authorities, then that -- I certainly didn't ask him that. That would misstate the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic? Is it Croatian authorities or Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a brief remark. We -- can we remove this text from the screen. I asked whether the then Serbian authorities stoked the fears of the Serb population, their fears from the Ustasha movement and the new Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did Serbian authorities -- did anything to inflame the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian authorities did not stoke the fears of the population. They just portrayed the political developments exactly as they happened, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I have finished with my redirect. I have no further questions for Mr. Licina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: As long as we have this document on the screen, may I, Mr. Licina, ask you about the last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's no longer on my screen, if we can put it back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Then ask what you said and -- so I can read that. You talked about the referendum and the plebiscite of the Serbian people in the Krajina showed, it says, you said, according to this document that the Serbs in Croatia are both for Croatia and for Yugoslavia. Democracy allows various options. Can you explain --

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's somewhere at the bottom of the page, which is not shown on the screen. It's towards the end of the whole speech, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It was -- in your concluding remarks you said that. Could you comment in a short way? Did this refer also to what originally in the assembly of Srb, the declaration said? Was it also originally, according to the declaration of Srb, one of the options for the political future of the Serbs in Croatia, to have a -- to live in a common state with the Serbs within the borders of the former socialist Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The fact is that we were working for the survival of the federation and, failing that, we advocated only a form of cultural autonomy. If there should be a rearrangement of the state then we would have wanted a greater degree of autonomy. I have already stated in this speech that we were both working for Croatia and for Yugoslavia because at that time Croatia was a state of both the Croatian and the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes, but we discussed that already yesterday. Now you expressed again something like a preference between these two options, a federation and confederation. You remember yesterday? But as you said it in the Croatian parliament and, as I understand it from the declaration of Srb, these were two equal options, separate, independent state of Croatia within the borders of the socialist Republic of Croatia and from the Yugoslavia federation. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were talking about the attitude of Serbs in Croatia towards the state of Croatia and how that would change in various options of the resolution of the crisis. If the state should remain a federation, we wanted cultural autonomy. If it is a confederation, we wanted territorial autonomy. And in case of secession, complete secession, then we wanted equal rights in terms of self-determination, as the Croats had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That is now a complicated sentence. In case of separation, we -- as you said that also in the parliament, you wanted the same rights as the Croats but not in terms of self-determination. Leaving that apart, the right to a secession, don't the Croats enjoy the same rights as the Serbs enjoy? Don't they enjoy the same rights as the Croats within the state of Croatia, under the Croatian constitution of December 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the constitution of December 1990, the Serbs no longer had the same rights. The only ones who had sovereignty vested in them were the Croats, the Croatian nation, because the new constitution defined Croatia as the state of the Croatian people. In all the prior constitutions, on the other hand, it stated that Croatia was a state of the Croatian people and the Serbian people in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I ask you, you stated in this new Croatian constitution, the Serbs were and are regarded a minority, not a nation. Is this your interpretation or is it expressed in the said constitution, that Croats -- that the Serbs are called a minority?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that constitution, it is clearly stated that Croatia is a state of the Croatian people, full stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: It doesn't mention --

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs as such are not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You think they are not mentioned at all, you want to say? They are also not mentioned as a minority or as a nation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In that provision, in that paragraph, Serbs are not mentioned at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Maybe in another paragraph or another provision, but that doesn't import right now or just a general explanation, please. Are the Serbs regarded as a minority, expressly, in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs are not referred to anywhere, Serbs as such. Only Croats are mentioned as a constituent nation, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When minorities are dealt with, there is no reference to them either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. In your studies in Zagreb, when you studied economy, economics, did you have law classes as well?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for a course in law, there was only one subject in the curriculum but that was back in secondary school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No, I didn't talk of the secondary school but of the university study of economics. Do I understand you correctly, you didn't have any legal subjects?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. So I've finished that point. May I go back to that constitutional issues but not in a too technical way? As to the former constitutional order of the socialist Republic of Croatia, are you, Mr. Licina, aware of how the coat of arms of this former socialist Republic of Croatia looked like? You commented today in the re-examination on the flag but let's talk about the coat of arms. We saw it on a document on Monday. It was the document legitimising your party, and on the upper left corner there was this coat of arms but it was very small and black and white only. So in the B/C/S original, we could see it but could you explain a little better how this coat of arms looked like?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The coat of arms of the socialist Republic of Croatia, if I remember well, was edged with wheat and at the top there was a five-pointed star, and in the middle, there was a picture of this Croatian chequerboard emerging from the sea. It's just the layout of red and white spots. It's not the same as the recent chequerboard flag, as the Ustasha chequerboard flag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And the chequerboard flag of today of the Republic of Croatia, is it the layout of the socialist republic's chequerboard symbol or of the Ustasha symbol?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The current layout is the same as in the one of the socialist republic. But the general appearance is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the origin, can you tell us a little bit about the origin of this chequerboard symbol. That was not in the Ustasha time, I suppose, so since when, to your knowledge, has this chequerboard symbol in history been used?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not a historian by training and I cannot give you that information. I know that the chequerboard appeared also in some form in the coat of arms of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia before the Second World War. It was one of the coat of arms. Whether it appeared in later periods, I don't know. I really can't tell you about things I don't know anything about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I have one question again to the referendum of August 1990. You said this referendum was held, I quote, "In all Serb municipalities where Serbs were in power." But then you also mentioned large cities, in particular Zagreb, and that Serbs were being prevented by force from voting. So who held actually this referendum, and in what parts of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The referendum was declared. In fact it was a public vote, not a referendum. It was declared on the whole territory of Croatia, in all places where we were physically able to conduct it, in places where Serbs were a majority it was organised by municipalities, and the Serbian Democratic Party or some Serbian societies, cultural societies, organised it in places where Serbs were a minority. It was organised in so-called urban areas of Croatia where Serbs were in the same numbers as in Krajina. According to our figures there were around 100.000 Serbs in the area of Zagreb alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I asked you who held this referendum or this initiative, however we want to call it. So it's the Serbian Democratic Party who held that? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The referendum was declared by the Serbian National Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So it was declared by the Serbian National Council, to be held in all Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that that was then a little difficult to organise that in places outside the SAO, but -- and then what would you regard it, in your eyes, the legal nature of this referendum? And to whom, lastly, was it addressed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I said earlier, I think it was back in examination-in-chief, the purpose was to show the will of the Serbian people. At the time Croatian authorities were trying to portray it as the opinion of only a minority of Serbs as represented by five MPs in the assembly. Our intent was to show that the majority of Serb people in Croatia supported that position, and the public vote did indeed show it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: To whom did you want to show that? I asked you, to whom was it addressed. To whom did you want to show that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To everybody, the Croatian authorities, the international public, everybody. A certain crisis had started. It was already underway. And what was in issue was whether it was just a minority within the Serbian population that held that view, and the public vote or the referendum showed that it was the position of the majority of the Serbian people in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean was the opinion of the majority of the Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With this public vote of the 19th of August, the Serbian people voted for Serbian sovereignty and Serbian autonomy, in the degree discussed before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And I suppose you presented this result also to the parliament in Zagreb in a formal way, or did you just mention it in this speech we saw?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those figures were presented in the Croatian assembly as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Was it addressed to the Serbian Assembly -- to the Croatian Assembly as a petition or whatever or what was the legal nature in relation to the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember how that technical arrangement was made, how it was practically done, but -- I can't tell you now, but I know that the Croatian assembly was informed about this public vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And then if I remember correctly, you said you went to this session of the assembly alone, without the other deputies of your party; is that correct? And how many of the deputies again were of your party members of the parliament?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Why didn't all of the five go there? Could you summarise the reasons for that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, some people were afraid to go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. And now, as to your function as a deputy in the Croatian parliament, how long did you -- have you been this representative, technically?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technically, formally speaking, until the next elections in Croatia. I don't remember when they were held because we no longer participated but my last actual attend dance was in December of 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Did you receive also some salary throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Later on I began receiving salary but not the salary per se but some expenses were paid out, since we came infrequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, as a last question, may I ask you, how did you get to know the accused, Mr. Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I met President Martic soon after I went to the parliament. We met several days later in Knin, and that's when we were introduced to each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So when about, in which month of which year?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the end of August or in early September 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Licina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Just a few questions. Some of them will touch on the same area as Judge Hoepfel has been questioning you in respect of, Mr. Licina. But for my education, you mentioned being a deputy in the assembly. What exactly is this office, a deputy what?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not clear who you have in mind or which assembly exactly because I was a deputy with several.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: In the Croatian assembly. You were a member and you were -- the term "deputy" is also referred to. Now, I can understand "member" but "deputy"? What functions would a deputy perform? I'm interested to know.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Croatian parliament, I was elected a deputy, or a member. A member of one of the three councils of the parliament, the municipal council, the council of municipalities and another two. I was elected a member to the Croatian parliament within that council of municipalities for the municipality of Gracac. That was the only title I had in the parliament, the only function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And you have stated that in the Croatian constitution, the new Croatian constitutions -- constitution, rather, Serbs were not specifically referred to anywhere; is that correct? That is your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What I would like to find out from you, you have said you're not a lawyer, you didn't study law, but you have given evidence in relation to the constitution, so I'd like to find this out from you: Is there anything in the constitution that prevents an interpretation that where the word "Croatia" or "Croatian" is spoken of, it does not include persons of all ethnicities, of all ethnic groups, that is Croatians as well as Serbs, and any other ethnic groups? That's what I want to find out from you, you having said that Serbs are not specifically referred to.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In order to have something put the way you put it, then it should have been stated that the Croatian state was the state of Croatian citizens. That would have been the correct way. But the way it was formulated, as a matter of fact, was that the Croatian state is the state of the Croatian people. Therefore, the first interpretation should have included Croatian citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So your understanding of the word "people" is that it would exclusively mean persons who were ethnic Croats? Is that correct? That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Otherwise it should have been put, "the citizens of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just take off exactly from where Judge Nosworthy left off, would the term "Croatian people" also not refer to the people of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Explicitly it is put the way that it is actually the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is the difference between Croatian people and the people of Croatia, in meaning?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should read, "The citizens of Croatia." If we say Croatian people that means only ethnic Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please try to focus on my question. I know what you say it should read. My question to you is, what is the substantive difference between Croatian people and people of Croatia? Even linguistically, what is the difference?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we talk about Croat people, these are ethnic Croats, and the people of Croatia need not be only from the -- from within Croatia, whereas the people of Croatia live within the boundaries of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, please listen to my question. I'm not talking about Croat people. I'm talking about Croatian people and the people of Croatia. What is the difference between those two terms?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the then Serbo-Croat language, the term "Croatian people" must be ethnic Croatian, and the citizens of Croatia or the people of Croatia includes everyone living in Croatia. This is as good as I can put it in linguistic terms, although this is my interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. In your evidence, and I think this was -- it may have been during -- no, it was during your evidence-in-chief, you said that barricades were a logical defensive measure and hence they threatened nobody. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do you remember that you were saying that these -- you were not party to the establishment of these barricades because they sprung in an unorganised fashion by civilian people. When you nod, it is not recorded on the transcript that you are answering, so if you nod, please say something also to indicate your nod.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was waiting for the interpretation. As I said, we didn't participate in the setting up of barricades. They simply sprang up. As for myself, I returned from the -- from Zagreb at the time by which the barricades had already sprung up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. Okay. Now, my question to you, then, is: If you didn't participate and they were not organised officially, how do you know that they were established with a defensive motive?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because at that time I resided there. I had regular contact with the people there. I knew how they felt, and it was clear to me why they put up those barricades. They were created out of fear, as a way of protection against a possible attack against those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And at that time, when these people did that, as you say it was not organised by the authorities, obviously they were taking the law into their hands, were they not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't exactly describe that as such. It was a reaction out of fear but certainly one could interpret it the way you did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but are you saying that, if I were a citizen of The Hague I could just go outside and start stopping cars without sanction from the local authorities to do so? And that would not be seen as illegal?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it in a different way. A citizen of The Hague -- of course, the authorities should sanction any such behaviour in which anyone puts up a barricade but the context was completely different there and then, in terms of security and politics. It is a very different context from the one that you've just described, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can go back to that context. Who -- who, in a state, is responsible for the security of the citizens, the individual members of the citizen or the individual members of the citizen -- I beg your pardon, individual members of the state or is it them through governmental authorities?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course authorities are responsible but, in this case, the authorities behaved in an opportune way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why? Why did they behave in that way?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the Croatian authorities in mind. They became -- they behaved adventuristically. They started disarming police stations and this caused unrest. It was a gung-ho --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm having in mind the Krajina authorities, the SAO Krajina authorities. They are in control of this area. People are -- the citizens are just mushrooming with blockades, and they don't seem to be taking any action to stop this apparently illegal action.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, at that time there was no Krajina. It was the 17th of August and the SAO Krajina was formed on the 19th of December. There was no Krajina. There were only Serbian municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's then go to -- sorry. You say this was in August, 17th of August. You testified that -- in terms of Exhibit 141, that that -- the declaration by the Serb people on their sovereignty and autonomy was adopted at an assembly held in Srb on the 25th of July 1990, am I right? From that day on, based on that declaration, how did the Serbian people regard the government to be run in the area where they declared their autonomy and sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb Assembly in Srb was a great national rally. It was used to found the Serb National Council as its executive body. However, at that time, Krajina wasn't marked off and wasn't carved out of Croatia. This was only to declare the will of the Serbian people as regards their sovereignty and autonomy. And the other thing happened some 20 days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question still stands: How did the Serbian people then anticipate government to be run in the area where they have declared their sovereignty and autonomy, whether or not that area is designated by a name, SAO Krajina, or not? But where are they having this sovereignty and where are they having this autonomy? It cannot be in the air, can it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The proclamation or the declaration defined the Serb people as a sovereign people in the entire territory of the Republic of Croatia. As of the moment when the central republican authorities introduced any changes, as of that moment, the area was to be defined. But at that time, the Republic of Croatia was still part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is something I do not understand. You say the proclamation defined the Serb people as a sovereign people in the entire territory of the Republic of Croatia. I thought it was also your evidence that your declaration included a rejection of the constitutional amendments by the Croatian parliament. Am I right? You stuck to the old constitution and not the new one.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct. Until then, the Serbian people were a sovereign people. With the new laws in Croatia and the new amendments to the constitution, everything was moving along the line of taking that sovereign status away from the Serb people. At the assembly in Srb, the Serbian people declared their sovereignty and they rejected such policies and attitude of Croatia. We still abided by the positive regulations and laws of Croatia but we rejected those which denied our sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Therefore, you saw yourself having a certain set of rules that governed the areas where the Serb people were staying in Croatia, which rules were distinct from the rules set up by the Croatian parliament, is that not so? When I talk of rules, I'm talking of laws of the government.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you say is correct only to the extent in which the Croatian state attempted to take away our right to be sovereign. We wanted to retain that and it was our right to be a sovereign people within that republic. We simply reacted after some political moves by Croatia. Their moves came first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I invite you once again to listen closely to my question and let's take it one step at a time. Let's not go back once we have passed the stage. I understand that you are saying the Serbs had problems with the way the Croats were taking their rights away. I'm saying, as a reaction to that, you had an assembly on the 25th of July 1990 in Srb. You made a declaration of autonomy and sovereignty, and that declaration rejected the newly amended constitution of Croatia. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The declaration rejected the amendments and not the constitution itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I mean. Fine. To the extent that you do not subordinate the Serb people to the newly amended constitution, as amended, to that extent, you then had to replace the rejected constitution with a set of rules that governed the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We applied the laws that were in place until that moment, and the constitution, and we chose not to implement the newly adopted amendments. So we focused on the very amendments and certain pieces of legislation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But to the extent that you adopted the law that was applicable up to that stage, it was a law as the Serb people have adopted it. It's now going to be implemented by the Serb people, not by the Croat people, because some other parts of the Croat law the Serb people don't want. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. We didn't want to deny the Croatian people their right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. Now, if I am right, and it means that where the Serb people were, the laws were being implemented by the Serb people, whether it is the acceptable part of the Croatian constitution or the replacement of the rejected part, that law is now being implemented by the Serbs - is that not so? - because they are now sovereign and autonomous of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb people were sovereign all along. Through this declaration we mainly tried to preserve our sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand all that, but now that you have preserved it by way of this declaration you now implement your own laws. Am I right? It's a very simple question, Mr. Licina.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time we did not put any laws into force. The only document that came out of that was the declaration. We didn't pass any new laws between the 25th of July and the 17th of August 1990. It was only the declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, I understand that. All I'm saying is that whatever laws were applicable in the area occupied by the Serbs, those laws from the 25th of July 1990, were now being implemented by the Serb people. Is that correct or is that not correct? I'm asking you a question. I would like you to clear me here.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We only chose to an abide by the old affirmative regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if that is correct that these laws, whatever the laws were where they were, were being implemented by the Serb people, my question is: When the citizens of these areas that are occupied by the Serbs and those citizens who were not in control decide to set up barricades, what did the implementers of the Serbian law in those areas then do about this apparent illegal activity on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, at that time, there were no Serb institutions in place. They were in the process of formation. They started existing basically as of December. I understand the gist of your question, but this was a turbulent time and some things were probably illegal, whereas others were legal, but this was quite a specific situation. That's what I'm trying to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I hear what you say. Now, at that time, before you established legal institutions and having declared and reaffirmed your sovereignty and autonomy, who took responsibility for law and order in these areas where the Serbs were living? That is between the 25th of July 1990 and December when you established some institutions. Who was taking responsibilities for the law at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the local authorities were responsible, the authorities in municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And who were the local authorities in municipalities?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To a certain degree, but also the Croatian authorities were responsible. There was a sort of joint, co-responsibility there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you -- the assembly had rejected the Croatians now. You are now -- have asserted your own autonomy and your sovereignty. Now, the local municipalities, the local authorities that you referred to as municipalities, these were not the authorities that set up the barricades, according to your evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And these local municipalities, am I right to venture that they were in the control of Serbs, particularly these municipalities that finally formed the SAO Krajina, because this is where the barricades, I suppose, were established?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what you are explaining to me actually it's a matter of the formation of dual authorities. So you're setting off from the 19th of December. On the 19th of December, the SAO Krajina is forming its authorities. In December the Republic of Croatia adopts its constitution without the Serbs. Up until that time the constitution still included Serbs. So there was no need for the Serbs not to recognise such a Croatia. But the declaration of the assembly in Srb proclaimed that if any constitutional changes took place leading to an eventual loss of constitutivity, then the amendments to the constitution would mean that there was a loss of sovereignty. Certain amendments did not actually imply a loss of sovereignty. But this loss of sovereignty did take effect after December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I plead with you. Let us stay consistent. You have said to me those were turbulent times and the context was different, it couldn't be the same as in The Hague. You have said to me that because of that turbulence, things didn't always go right. Now, surely, the fundamental cause of the turbulence here, or the fundamental result of the turbulence, is that the Serb population is rejecting any authority by the Croat government and, therefore, it becomes inconceivable to expect that the Serb people would accept any authority by the Croatian government. You've walked out of their parliament. You don't want them. You've rejected them. Now, somebody must fill the vacuum. Now there is a governmental vacuum between the 25th of July 1990 and the 5th of December when you adopt your institution, physically, on the ground. Somebody must take responsibility for law and order in the areas that are controlled by the Serbs now, where the Serbs have now reaffirmed their sovereignty and autonomy. Now, you've told me it's the municipalities. It cannot -- you can't reaffirm your sovereignty and autonomy and still expect joint rule from the person that you are affirming yourself against. I expect that in the spirit of this affirmation, you would assert your authority over the area that you rule. Isn't that logical? Isn't that consistent with your -- the whole initiative?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I left the Croatian assembly on the 24th of December 1990, the day before the constitution of Croatia was adopted. Up until that time, Croatia was a state of both the Croatian and the Serbian people. With the adoption of the constitution in December 1990, it definitely ceases to be a state of the Serbian people. The declaration from the Srb assembly declared that if this were to take place, then Serbs would form their own autonomy. They did not form their own autonomy until the 19th of December, on the eve of the adoption of the new Croatian constitution. Up until that time, there was no autonomy. Up until that time, in accordance with that proclamation the Serbs had cultural autonomy, as we called it. That was the aspiration that we are in favour of our own script, our own language, and so on. Up until that time we did not wish to break off from Croatia. But we said that if there was to be a separation, then there would be autonomy. If Croatia were to adopt a constitution in which the Serbs would not be a constituent people, then the Serbs would in the territorial sense, declare autonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are moving far away from my question. Let me try and put the question differently. How did you expect the Croatian authorities to come and maintain law and order in an area occupied by a Serb population that has declared itself, on the 25th of July 1990, to be rejecting the very laws that the Croatian authorities would have to implement in this area of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the declaration from the Srb assembly was not something whereby the Serb people declared themselves as something. They just affirmed something that already was in existence, the autonomy. So the Srb assembly declaration states that in the event of the new Croatian constitution not being the state of Serbian people as well, in that case, Serbs would have their own autonomy. This is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll abandon that issue at this point and ask you the next question. Your evidence has been to the effect that Croatia could not decide to secede from the SFRY without the consent of the Serbs, could not legitimately do so without the consent of the Serbs who are in Croatia. Is that a correct interpretation of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbian people is one of the two constituent peoples so its agreement is required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Therefore it was wrong in your interpretation of the Croats to try to secede from the SFRY without the necessary consent of the Serbs. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We are not disputing the rights of the Croats as a people to secede or to embark on self-determination. That is their right. We never disputed the right of the Croatian people to self-determination. All we were doing is seeking the same right for ourselves, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no. You don't understand. The Croatian people want to take Croatia, the land, out of the federation of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia. Am I right? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Representatives of the Croatian authorities, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in this country, this portion of land called Croatia, there are also Serb people who are citizens of Croatia, and without whose consent this decision to take Croatia out cannot legitimately be taken, am I right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You would have the same case in Belgium, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this is so because both Serbs and Croats are constituent nations within Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you, then, is: How do the Serbs establish an SAO Krajina without the consent of the Croats? You're doing exactly the same thing that you are accusing the Croats of having done vis-a-vis the SFRY. Why do you do it and not seek the consent of the Croats to establish the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it were to be that way, then we would be going around in circles. The rights of one people and the other people both exist, the right of the Serbian and the right of the Croatian people. We are not disputing their rights. In that case, Croatia as such would need to re-compose itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's the end of my questions. We'll adjourn. We'll come back tomorrow morning. Tomorrow is Friday. Is it in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one thing, very briefly. Mr. Licina's departure has been postponed on a number of times. The Victims and Witnesses Unit has postponed his flight twice already. According to the information of the Defence team, Mr. Licina is due to leave tomorrow afternoon. Since the Chamber has finished asking its questions, I'm just going to say that the Defence has no questions arising from the questions of the Judges. I don't know if the Prosecution has questions arising from your questions. I apologise to the other side but I'm just making a best attempt to complete the examination of the witness today so that we would not need to postpone his departure tomorrow. I'm just trying to save expenses for the Tribunal and just to let you know what the situation is at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I do have a few questions but I don't think it would cause him to miss a flight in the afternoon, by any stretch of the imagination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unfortunately the Prosecution has some questions to put and unfortunately we can't go much further. Judge Nosworthy must be back in court at quarter past two, unfortunately, so we've got to release her. But as the Prosecution says, they will finish very early tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I'm very grateful. I just wanted to inform you of the situation. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned. Come back tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 18th day of August, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
